_title: 7 Days Interrailing Through Italy (2026) — WoW Train · glosx.app
_desc: A complete 7-day Italy by train itinerary: Rome, Florence, Venice and the Cinque Terre. Practical tips, timings and booking advice.
b1: 7 Days Interrailing Through Italy: A Perfect Train Itinerary
b2: By WoW Train · June 2026 · 7 min read
b3: Italy is made for the train. Fast lines link the great cities in a couple of hours, and a short regional hop drops you into the cliffs of the Cinque Terre. Here's a relaxed but complete one-week route — Rome, Florence, Venice and the coast — that you can ride entirely by rail.
b8: Day 5: Florence → Cinque Terre (~2h 30m via La Spezia)
b9: Day 6: Cinque Terre → Venice (~5h with a change in Milan or Florence)
b12: Start in the capital. Two days is enough for the essentials: the Colosseum and Roman Forum, the Pantheon, Trastevere at dusk, and an early morning at the Vatican before the crowds. Stay near Roma Termini — it's the main station and the hub for everything that comes next.
b14: One of Europe's great fast-train rides. Frecciarossa (Trenitalia) and Italo both run Rome–Florence in about 1 hour 30 minutes, at up to 300 km/h. Trains leave Roma Termini and arrive at Firenze Santa Maria Novella, a 10-minute walk from the Duomo.
b15: Book a morning train and you'll be eating lunch in Florence. Fares from €20–€30 if you book ahead; closer to departure they climb past €50.
b17: Renaissance central. Climb the Duomo, see Michelangelo's David, walk the Ponte Vecchio and watch the sunset from Piazzale Michelangelo. Florence is compact and walkable — no need for transit inside the city.
b19: The scenic highlight. Take a train to La Spezia Centrale (around 2h 30m, usually via Pisa), then switch to the Cinque Terre Express — the little regional line that stitches together the five cliffside villages: Riomaggiore, Manarola, Corniglia, Vernazza and Monterosso.
b20: A Cinque Terre Card gives you unlimited hops between the villages all day, so you can village-hop without buying a ticket each time. It's one of the most beautiful short rides in Italy.
b22: The longest leg of the week — roughly 5 hours with one change, usually in Milan or back through Florence onto a Frecciarossa. Trains arrive at Venezia Santa Lucia, and the moment you step out the Grand Canal is right there. No cars, no taxis — just water.
b24: Finish slowly. St Mark's Square early before the day-trippers, a vaporetto down the Grand Canal, and the back canals of Cannaregio or Dorsoduro where the city feels local again.
b25: Which trains, and how to keep costs down
b26: High-speed (Frecciarossa, Italo): book the long city-to-city legs 3–6 weeks ahead for the cheapest fares — prices are dynamic and rise toward departure.
b27: Regional trains (like the Cinque Terre Express): fixed price, no need to book in advance — just buy on the day.
b28: Validate regional tickets before boarding if your ticket isn't time-stamped.
b29: Travel city-centre to city-centre — Italian stations are central, so you skip airport transfers entirely.
b31: Booked ahead, the four train legs above typically total around €90–€130 per person for the week — less than a couple of short flights, and far more scenic.
b32: The tricky part of a trip like this is juggling several operators and live times across the week.
